title: Poll-of-polls and seat forecast: 2026 New Zealand general election
how_to_read: The poll average is where the public polls, adjusted for each pollster's habitual lean, put each party today. Its interval shows only how noisy the polls are.
The forecast interval is wider: it adds how far New Zealand's final polls have missed the result at the last five elections and how much support can still move before 7 November.

Seats come from running the real MMP rules (5% or an electorate seat, Sainte-Laguë, overhang) on tens of thousands of simulated results. Expected seats are an average; the 80% range is where 8 in 10 simulations land.
A bloc's 'majority' probability is the share of simulations in which those parties alone hold more than half of all seats, including overhang seats.
Probabilities are rounded to the nearest 1% and seats to whole numbers deliberately: the inputs are not precise enough to justify more.
A 70% chance is not a certainty: it means the other outcome happens about 3 times in 10.

blocs.bloc: Labour + Green + Te Pāti Māori + TOP

majority_threshold.note: 61 of 120; one more for every two overhang seats (62 of 122-123)

most_likely_parliament.note: The single most frequent exact seat combination across 40,000 simulations; with seven parties even the modal combination occurs in well under 1% of them, so read it as one plausible parliament, not a prediction.

pollsters.commissioner: Anacta Consulting (corporate clients; has polled for Labour)
Talbot Mills Research (corporate-client poll; also Labour's pollster, formerly UMR)
Curia Market Research (National's pollster) - publicly released polls not sponsored by the Taxpayers' Union

house_effects_note: House effect = that pollster's average deviation from the pooled trend this term, after shrinkage, in percentage points; positive = the pollster runs high for that party. Constrained to average zero across the independent public pollsters (1 News–Verian, RNZ–Reid Research, Roy Morgan, Taxpayers' Union–Curia, The Post/Freshwater Strategy), so they describe relative leans, not absolute bias. Party-commissioned/corporate polls (internal=true) get half weight and do not anchor the average.
undecided_note: All NZ pollsters publish party shares with undecided voters (typically 5-15%) excluded, so polls already sum to ~100% of decided voters and the aggregate is used as published. 'Others' are implied as 100 minus the seven listed parties. The historical calibration measures the resulting error directly, so no separate undecided adjustment is applied.

calibration.method: Final-3-weeks pooled average (sqrt(n) weights, no house adjustment) vs official result, per party; error SD modelled as k*sqrt(p(100-p))/10 fitted by least squares on squared errors (so historical bias widens the spread rather than shifting the mean).
calibration.correlation_note: Pairwise correlation of final-poll errors across the five elections (pairs with at least four shared elections), shrunk by n/(n+3) because five observations cannot pin down a correlation; matrix forced positive-definite.
calibration.drift_note: Random-walk innovation variance per day, estimated from week-to-week changes in this term's own trend (half attributed to real movement). Multiplied by days to the election.

electorates.note: Only electorates that can change the seat allocation are simulated: Epsom (ACT's insurance seat) and the seven Māori seats (Te Pāti Māori's party vote is far below 5%, so every seat it wins is an overhang seat; an independent or Te Tai Tokerau Party winner also changes the arithmetic). General seats won by National, Labour or the Greens are assumed never to exceed those parties' list entitlement, so they do not affect totals.

epsom.assumption: David Seymour (ACT) won Epsom by 8,142 votes in 2023 over Paul Goldsmith (National), who is standing again; National has not formally stood aside but did not campaign hard for the seat in 2023. ACT is polling 9-11% so Epsom only matters if ACT fell below 5%. Set at 90% (no 2026 Epsom poll).

Hauraki-Waikato.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=500) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

maori_seats_context: 2023: Te Pāti Māori won 6 of 7 (Tāmaki Makaurau by 42 votes, Te Tai Tokerau by 517); Labour held Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.
6 Sep 2025 Tāmaki Makaurau by-election: Oriini Kaipara (TPM) 6,948 beat Peeni Henare (Labour) 3,429 (turnout low). Kaipara stands again; Labour's candidate is Kerrin Leoni.

Nov 2025: Tākuta Ferris (Te Tai Tonga) and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi (Te Tai Tokerau) were expelled from TPM; Kapa-Kingi was reinstated by the High Court, then left in May 2026 to found Te Tai Tokerau Party. Ferris stands as an independent.
Prior for Te Tai Tokerau and Te Tai Tonga: half of the 2023 Te Pāti Māori candidate vote is credited to the sitting MP's new vehicle (Te Tai Tokerau Party / independent) and half to Te Pāti Māori.
Electorate polls in Māori seats have small samples (n≈500) and a history of large misses; the 9-point systematic error term and the 30% weight on the 2023 result reflect that.

historical_track_record.note: What this model would have said two weeks before each election since 2011 (polls as of that date, house effects estimated from that term, calibration from the other four elections) versus the official result; plus the final-3-weeks simple pooled average, and how the governing party moved from mid-term (18 months out) to polling day.

caveats: Polling error: at the last five elections NZ's final polls missed individual parties by up to 5 points (National 2020). The forecast intervals are built from those misses, but a miss bigger than any since 2011 is always possible.

Threshold effects: TOP and NZ First sit near the 5% line, and Te Pāti Māori's seats depend on a handful of Māori-electorate contests. A one-point shift can move 6-10 seats between blocs, which is why the bloc probabilities are far less certain than the vote shares.
Electorate assumptions: Epsom and the Māori seats are modelled from very few, small-sample electorate polls and stated assumptions; those probabilities are the model's weakest input.
Late swing: a fifth of voters typically decide in the final fortnight; advance voting (which opened 26 Oct) blunts but does not remove this.
Undecideds: polls exclude 5-15% undecided voters; if they break unevenly the published shares shift.
House effects are relative to the average public pollster, not to the truth; if all pollsters share a bias (as in 2020) the aggregate shares it.
Party-commissioned and corporate-client polls (Talbot Mills, Anacta, Curia) are published selectively and are down-weighted, but may still colour the average.
The model does not forecast coalition negotiations: a 'majority' means the seats exist, not that the parties would agree to govern together.
Only seven parties are modelled; a minor party winning an electorate or crossing 5% from nowhere is not simulated.

simulation.distribution: multivariate logit-normal around the poll average
